scope: All 15 current Estonian county flag meaning records, corresponding images and internal SVG metadata. Municipal flags, maps, population and city flags are outside this ledger.
method: Read all 15 complete English descriptions and Estonian Government Office blazons/explanations.
Downloaded and visually compared all 15 official SVGs with repository images.
Parsed all 15 SVG root identifiers and embedded descriptive metadata.
Read National Archives historical panels 2,6-1,9,10-1,12; all 22 panels downloaded, other panels only visually screened at contact-sheet scale.
Common statements counted once per record; some compound design claims remain grouped. This is not a universal atomic-claim denominator.
findings: F84: EE-57 eagle described as hawk
F85: EE-86 current sword direction described incorrectly
F86: EE-37 and EE-51 SVG root/layer identifiers say Flag of Elva
limits: No wholesale correctness certification of an entire record; unresolved claims retain their own status.
The 1939 shared-pattern date has primary archival support. The 1996/97 registrations largely remain secondary-corroborated.
Historical proposal artwork must not be confused with current statutory artwork.
A mismatch in legacy source filename/code alone does not establish a wrong flag; the visible county identity was separately checked.
No application content or image was changed.

applicationRecord.description: Hiiu County’s flag follows the common pattern of Estonia’s county flags, confirmed on 7 August 1939: two equal horizontal stripes, white over green, in the ratio 7:11, with the county’s arms at the centre of the white stripe as its distinguishing mark. It was registered on 25 November 1996. The arms show a vertical red rope tied in three knots between four red lilies on silver. The lilies, drawn from the arms of the Ungern-Sternberg family, stand for Hiiumaa’s four parishes. The rope comes from a legend in the collection Esivanemate varandus: an old man of Hiiumaa gave men from Tallinn, stranded on the island in distress at sea, a length of rope with three knots so that they would get home safely.

applicationRecord.description: Põlva County’s flag follows the common pattern of Estonia’s county flags, confirmed on 7 August 1939: two equal horizontal stripes, white over green, in the ratio 7:11, with the county’s arms at the centre of the white stripe as its distinguishing mark. It was registered on 7 November 1996. The arms show three black beavers sitting in a diagonal row on gold. Põlva is a newcomer to Estonia’s administrative map, just as beavers are newcomers to its wildlife: a native species that had vanished through heavy hunting. People and beavers here are said to share traits too: they keep somewhat to themselves, are tenacious and hard-working, and go their own way. There are three beavers because the county’s parishes were formed from three earlier administrative units.

applicationRecord.description: Tartu County’s flag follows the common pattern of Estonia’s county flags, confirmed on 7 August 1939: two equal horizontal stripes, white over green, in the ratio 7:11, with the county’s arms at the centre of the white stripe as its distinguishing mark. It was registered on 25 September 1996. The arms are divided diagonally, blue over green, by a silver wavy band carrying two blue wavy lines, with a gold six-pointed star above and a gold oak branch below; Günther Reindorff drew the present version in 1937. The elements go back to the county’s 1926 design, which explained the wavy band as the Emajõgi river that divides the county, the star as Tartu University spreading culture and education across Estonia, and the oak as the oak grove of Taara known from folk songs.

applicationRecord.description: Võru County’s flag follows the common pattern of Estonia’s county flags, confirmed on 7 August 1939: two equal horizontal stripes, white over green, in the ratio 7:11, with the county’s arms at the centre of the white stripe as its distinguishing mark. It was registered on 12 December 1996. The arms show, on blue, a gold ring and the silver sword of Kalevipoeg with a golden hilt, pointing downwards. Blue stands for a hopeful future and Võrumaa’s blue sky; the gold ring (võru) names the county, and the sword stands for its readiness to defend itself.
